name: Pitzen knot
steps: Pass the tag through the hook eye and back alongside the standing line.
Wrap the tag forward, away from the eye, three or four turns around the standing line.
Bring the tag back and pass it through the loop formed at the eye.
Wet it and pull the standing line to seat the knot tight against the eye.
Trim the tag close.
bestFor: Freshwater dries and nymphs — small, strong, and it seats clean on tiny hook eyes.
failsWhen: Seated dry, or drawn up by pulling the tag instead of the standing line.
notes: House rule: this is the freshwater fly knot. Do not mix a clinch into the rotation — one knot tied well beats two tied adequately.
sources: Allowance is a working convention, not a measured figure — practitioners use 1–6 in per end

name: Non-slip mono loop
steps: Tie a simple overhand knot in the tippet about six inches from the tag end, leaving it open.
Pass the tag through the hook eye and back through the overhand knot from the same side it exited.
Wrap the tag around the standing line — more turns for lighter tippet, fewer for heavy.
Bring the tag back through the overhand knot, entering the same side it originally exited.
Wet it, seat the wraps first, then pull the standing line to close the loop to size.
Trim the tag close.
bestFor: Every saltwater fly, and freshwater streamers — the loop lets a weighted fly swim and drop freely.
failsWhen: The tag re-enters the overhand from the wrong side, which quietly halves the strength.
notes: House rule: loop knot on all saltwater flies and all streamers. Wrap count varies with tippet weight — that is the part worth drilling. Orvis: 6 turns under 8 lb, 5 turns up to 40 lb. Start with about 10 in of tag — most of the allowance is grip, not knot.
sources: Allowance is a working convention, not a measured figure — practitioners use 1–6 in per end

name: Blood knot
steps: Overlap the two lines by several inches, facing opposite directions.
Wrap one tag around the other line five turns, then bring it back through the gap at the centre.
Wrap the second tag around the first line five turns in the opposite direction.
Pass it back through the same centre gap, from the opposite side.
Wet and pull both standing lines steadily until the wraps roll together.
Trim both tags.
bestFor: Joining leader sections of similar diameter — the tidiest option for a hand-built leader.
failsWhen: Diameters differ by more than about 0.002 in; use a surgeon's knot instead.
sources: Allowance is a working convention, not a measured figure — practitioners use 1–6 in per end
notes: Gary Borger's rule: an even blood knot seats up to a 0.002 in difference. For each further 0.002 in, the THIN side takes one more turn — that is the 5/7 blood knot.

name: Double surgeon's knot
steps: Lay the two lines alongside each other with a long overlap.
Form a loop with both lines together.
Pass both tag ends through the loop twice.
Wet it and pull all four ends at once to seat it evenly.
Trim both tags.
bestFor: Fast tippet changes on the water, and joining unequal diameters.
failsWhen: Only two of the four ends are pulled, which seats it crooked.
notes: The cold-hands, failing-light knot. Tolerates a diameter mismatch a blood knot will not, which is exactly when to reach for it.
sources: Allowance is a working convention, not a measured figure — practitioners use 1–6 in per end

name: Perfection loop
steps: Form a loop with the tag behind the standing line.
Form a second, smaller loop in front of the first, holding both.
Bring the tag between the two loops.
Pass the second loop through the first.
Wet and pull the new loop and the standing line apart to seat.
Trim the tag.
bestFor: The butt-end loop on a hand-built leader, for loop-to-loop onto the fly line.
failsWhen: Seated without wetting in heavy butt material, which cuts itself.
sources: Allowance is a working convention, not a measured figure — practitioners use 1–6 in per end

name: Nail knot
steps: Lay a small tube alongside the fly line tip and the leader butt.
Wrap the leader butt around line and tube six or seven turns, working toward the line tip.
Feed the tag back through the tube and withdraw the tube.
Pull the wraps snug a little at a time, alternating ends.
Seat hard, trim both tags, and coat if you want it to shoot cleanly.
bestFor: A permanent butt section on a fly line with no welded loop.
failsWhen: Wraps cross over one another instead of lying side by side.
notes: A vise-and-coffee-table knot, not a knot to learn on the water.
sources: Allowance is a working convention, not a measured figure — practitioners use 1–6 in per end

name: Albright knot
steps: Form a loop in the heavier line.
Pass the lighter line through the loop and wrap it back over both legs, ten turns, working toward the loop's end.
Feed the tag back out through the loop the same side it entered.
Wet, seat the wraps down the loop, then pull both standing lines.
Trim both tags.
bestFor: Joining wildly unequal diameters — class tippet to a heavy bite section.
failsWhen: Wraps slide off the end of the loop under load because they were never seated.
notes: Only needed once tarpon are genuinely on the calendar. Built for wildly unequal diameters — class tippet to a heavy bite section.
sources: Allowance is a working convention, not a measured figure — practitioners use 1–6 in per end
